16. Longitudinal data: from events to analysis

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-16-longitudinal.Rmd
book-16-longitudinal.Rmd

What you will learn

Choose wide, long or person-period data; handle irregular measurements and missing periods; reshape privately; and fit a discrete-time hazard model and repeated-measure mixed models across two connections.

You need: Before you start, output formats and lab values. Start a fresh session in book-work and run every section in order, including solutions. GiBleed and Synthea are public synthetic resources. Their results teach analysis mechanics, not clinical conclusions. This chapter uses dsBaseClient 6.3.5.

Concept selections refer to the searches and saved definitions in chapter 4, including the separate questionnaire catalogue. Additional body-measurement concepts are found on screen in the formula walkthrough.

The same people, two shapes

Longitudinal means following the same people over time. A small invented example: three people measured on two days. Days are relative to each person’s entry.

Person Value on day 0 Value on day 30
A 14 15
B 13 NA
C 15 14

Turning the two measurement columns into rows gives this long picture:

Person Day Value
A 0 14
A 30 15
B 0 13
B 30 NA
C 0 15
C 30 14

This is a scheduled grid: B’s second row explicitly represents a missing value. An event-long table would omit B’s day-30 row if no event occurred. Its absence must not be interpreted as a measured zero. Six rows still represent three people.

Exercise. Which shape would you use to compare baseline means? Which for a model of change over time?

Solution

Use the wide day-0 column for baseline means. Use long data with a person key and time for repeated-measure models. Account for dependence between the same person’s rows. Taking an ordinary mean over long rows weights frequent attenders more.

Choose the shape before requesting it

Question Shape What a row means
Baseline lab or cross-sectional comparison wide One person or entry episode
How do repeated readings vary with time? long One observed measurement, with time since index
Did an outcome occur during this at-risk period? person_period One person-episode and time bin
How long until the first outcome or censoring? survival One follow-up record
When was an exposure active? intervals One exposure start and end

Time-varying covariates belong to periods: use information available by that period’s start. A future lab mean would leak future information into a hazard model. A survival output must specify censoring. Intervals retain both ends of an exposure; they are not automatically nonoverlapping. Chapter 8 executes all five shapes.

Start with GiBleed and request visit rows directly from a recipe.

library(dsOMOPClient)
source("tools/book/display.R")
source("tools/book/connection.R")
source("tools/book/practice.R")
practice <- book_connect("gibleed")
conns <- practice$conns
visits <- omop_event("visit_occurrence", concepts = 9201L, name = "admission")
visitors <- omop_population("visitors", index = omop_index(visits))
visit_recipe <- omop_recipe(events = list(visits), populations = list(visitors),
  outputs = omop_output("visits", rows = "visitors", format = "long", sources = "admission",
    options = list(columns_derived = c("days_from_index", "duration_days"))))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(visit_recipe, out = c(visits = "D_visit_long"), conns = conns))
#>         visits 
#> "D_visit_long"

The long table remains private. Release only the named visit-type counts and column names, which describe the representation.

dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_visit_long", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#>  [1] "row_id"                  "cohort_row_id"           "person_id"              
#>  [4] "concept_id"              "start_date"              "end_date"               
#>  [7] "visit_type_concept_id"   "discharge_to_concept_id" "days_from_index"        
#> [10] "duration_days"
visit_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_visit_long$concept_id", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(visit_counts))
Category Count
Inpatient Visit 1037
NA 0

Exercise. Summarise the time since entry. Does a long format guarantee repeated visits?

Solution

visit_time <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_visit_long$days_from_index", type = "combine", datasources = conns)
visit_time
#> $Global.Mean
#>                 EstimatedMean Nmissing Nvalid Ntotal
#> studiesCombined      1272.554        0   1037   1037
#> 
#> $Nstudies
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $ValidityMessage
#>      ValidityMessage 
#> site "VALID ANALYSIS"

No. Here the mean is about 1273 days: the first admission contributes zero, and subsequent admissions contribute positive offsets. Some people still have only one admission. This is an event-weighted mean, not the mean gap between admissions. Switch to Synthea for repeated numeric measurements.

Irregular measurements: define windows first 

ds.omop.disconnect(conns = conns)
DSI::datashield.logout(conns)
practice <- book_connect("numeric")
conns <- practice$conns
lab <- omop_event("measurement", concepts = 3000963L, value = "value_as_number",
  where = omop_where(unit_concept_id == 8713L), name = "hb")
entry <- omop_population("entry", index = omop_index(lab))
class(entry)
#> [1] "omop_population" "list"

Index is each person’s first hemoglobin. These synthetic records are irregularly spaced over years. Use three 1000-day windows, not calendar years. Window 1 includes days 0–999, window 2 days 1000–1999, and window 3 days 2000–2999. First and last refer to actual dates within each window, not scheduled visits.

window_value <- function(which, start, end) {
  omop_variable(event = lab, reducer = omop_reduce(which,
    window = omop_window(start, end)))
}
windows <- omop_recipe(events = list(lab), populations = list(entry), variables = list(
  first1 = window_value("first_value", 0, 999),
  first2 = window_value("first_value", 1000, 1999),
  first3 = window_value("first_value", 2000, 2999),
  last1 = window_value("last_value", 0, 999),
  last2 = window_value("last_value", 1000, 1999),
  last3 = window_value("last_value", 2000, 2999)),
  outputs = omop_output("wide", rows = "entry", format = "wide"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(windows, out = c(wide = "D_windows"), conns = conns))
#>        wide 
#> "D_windows"

No eligible nonmissing value gives NA. It never gives zero hemoglobin. Before analysing a period, count its missing values and summarise its first and last readings. The following loop repeats the same three explicit aggregate calls.

window_results <- lapply(1:3, function(period) {
  first_name <- paste0("D_windows$first", period)
  last_name <- paste0("D_windows$last", period)
  first_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean(first_name, type = "combine", datasources = conns)
  last_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean(last_name, type = "combine", datasources = conns)
  data.frame(Period = period,
    First = first_mean$Global.Mean[1, 1], Last = last_mean$Global.Mean[1, 1],
    Observed = first_mean$Global.Mean[1, "Nvalid"], Missing = first_mean$Global.Mean[1, "Nmissing"])
})
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, window_results))
Period First Last Observed Missing
1 13.98571 14.28571 28 0
2 15.30000 15.30000 10 18
3 14.56667 14.56667 15 13

These means use the observed people in each period; changing means can therefore reflect changing membership. A missing measurement does not prove that the person left observation. Check observation coverage separately for a follow-up analysis.

Exercise. Make missingness a named category for each period and release its counts.

Solution

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_windows",
  missing1 = ifelse(is.na(first1), "missing", "observed"),
  missing2 = ifelse(is.na(first2), "missing", "observed"),
  missing3 = ifelse(is.na(first3), "missing", "observed"),
  newobj = "D_missing", conns = conns))
#> [1] "D_missing"
missing_counts <- lapply(1:3, function(period) {
  result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table(paste0("D_missing$missing", period), datasources = conns)
  transform(book_counts(result), Period = period)
})
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, missing_counts))
Category Count Period
observed 28 1
NA 0 1
missing 18 2
observed 10 2
NA 0 2
missing 13 3
observed 15 3
NA 0 3

The source checks find 28, 10 and 15 observed people: therefore 0, 18 and 13 missing values. Do not carry a measurement forward without declaring how long it remains valid and what that assumption means.

Wide columns at prespecified time points

A wide table can hold several scheduled values for each person. A named grid makes the target times, tolerances and selection rule explicit. Each value comes from an eligible observed event; no measurement is interpolated.

points <- omop_timepoints(list(
  baseline = omop_timepoint(),
  year3 = omop_timepoint(3, "years", tolerance = c(-365, 365))),
  anchor = "index", reuse = FALSE)
repeated_hb <- omop_repeated(lab, values = list(hb = omop_number_rows(lab)),
  timepoints = points, missing = "keep")
repeated_recipe <- omop_recipe(events = list(lab), populations = list(entry),
  variables = list(measurements = repeated_hb),
  outputs = omop_output("wide", rows = "entry", format = "wide"))
repeated_result <- recipe_execute(repeated_recipe, out = "D_timepoints", conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_timepoints", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"                   "cohort_row_id"            "person_id"               
#> [4] "measurements_hb_baseline" "measurements_hb_year3"

The generated names retain the measurement and time-point names. closest is the default selection; first or last would choose differently within the inclusive tolerance. reuse = FALSE prevents an event from filling two points. The tolerance here is a teaching choice for irregular data, not a claim that a lab a year away represents a clinical three-year visit.

Exercise. Inspect the baseline column’s released summary.

Solution: a scheduled column

knitr::kable(book_summary(dsBaseClient::ds.summary(
  "D_timepoints$measurements_hb_baseline", datasources = conns)))
Site Statistic Value
site 5% 11.29000
site 10% 12.48000
site 25% 12.97500
site 50% 13.70000
site 75% 15.42500
site 90% 16.19000
site 95% 16.85500
site Mean 13.98571

The baseline target is day zero at the first lab. Later targets without an eligible reading remain missing; they are not zero-valued measurements.

Exercise. Where can you check the expanded columns’ types before modelling?

Solution: the published table codebook

knitr::kable(recipe_codebook(repeated_result)[[1]]$columns[c("name", "r_type", "unit")])
name r_type unit
row_id character not_applicable
cohort_row_id character not_applicable
person_id character not_applicable
measurements_hb_baseline double unresolved_source
measurements_hb_year3 double unresolved_source

Use the numeric columns in a model only after choosing how to handle missing scheduled readings. A codebook does not expose their missingness frequency.

Ask the recipe, or reshape on the server

The installed ds.reShape() can turn existing wide columns into period rows. The native recipe uses names without dots. Create three private aliases with the first.1, first.2, first.3 names expected by this dsBase reshape method. This operation assigns privately; it never returns individual rows.

stopifnot(all(c("ds.reShape", "ds.lmerSLMA", "ds.glmerSLMA") %in%
                getNamespaceExports("dsBaseClient")))
for (period in 1:3) {
  dsBaseClient::ds.asNumeric(x.name = paste0("D_windows$first", period),
    newobj = paste0("first.", period), datasources = conns)
}
dsBaseClient::ds.dataFrame(c("D_windows$person_id", "first.1", "first.2", "first.3"),
  newobj = "D_for_reshape", datasources = conns)
#> $is.object.created
#> [1] "A data object <D_for_reshape> has been created in all specified data sources"
#> 
#> $validity.check
#> [1] "<D_for_reshape> appears valid in all sources"
dsBaseClient::ds.reShape("D_for_reshape", varying = c("first.1", "first.2", "first.3"),
  timevar.name = "period", idvar.name = "person_id", direction = "long",
  newobj = "D_reshaped", datasources = conns)
#> $is.object.created
#> [1] "A data object <D_reshaped> has been created in all specified data sources"
#> 
#> $validity.check
#> [1] "<D_reshaped> appears valid in all sources"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_reshaped", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id" "period"    "first"

This gives each person three period rows, including missing first values. Only the person key and three first values enter this reshape; last values are not copied into every period. Its period is 1, 2 or 3, not an actual measurement date. A reshape cannot recover dates or readings discarded by a reducer. ds.reShape also depends on the server’s allowed privacy profile; this run uses the installed practice configuration.

For a dense panel with last values and event counts, ask the recipe directly. The native panel supports last and mean, but not a first analysis. The wide window reducers above provide first values explicitly without inventing a panel option.

panel <- omop_recipe(events = list(lab), populations = list(entry),
  outputs = omop_output("panel", rows = "entry", format = "person_period",
    options = list(sources = list(lab), bins = list(width = 1000L),
      window = omop_window(0, 2999), analyses = c("count", "last"), representation = "dense")))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(panel, out = c(panel = "D_panel"), conns = conns))
#>     panel 
#> "D_panel"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_panel", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"            "cohort_row_id"     "person_id"         "period_start_days"
#> [5] "period_end_days"   "days"              "hb_count"          "hb_last"

The panel respects observation coverage and retains empty observed bins: a zero count and a missing last value describe different things. It can omit time outside coverage, so it need not have the same roster as the wide-window reshape. Requesting the right shape keeps keys, windows, coverage and event semantics in one checked plan.

Exercise. Verify that the reshape kept three rows per person, without reading rows.

Solution

period_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_reshaped$period", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(period_counts))
Category Count
1 28
2 28
3 28
NA 0

There are 28 rows in each period, including rows with missing measurements. That is 84 rows, still 28 people. A row-count increase is not a sample-size increase.

Build a risk set for a discrete-time hazard

A hazard is the probability of an outcome in the current period among people still at risk at its start. Here the outcome is the next recorded hemoglobin, not illness or death. Start on day 1 after the first reading, and stop at the first subsequent reading, death, observation end or day 7300, whichever comes first. The absence of a repeat lab is not a normal result.

For this section use the same disjoint public Synthea split as chapter 15: 14 people at each of two local DSLite servers. No people are duplicated. A real multisite study must establish nonoverlapping populations separately.

pair <- book_numeric_pair()
two_conns <- pair$conns
names(two_conns)
#> [1] "north" "south"

The panel already stops at observation coverage. Attach one first-outcome day and one death day per episode, using a checked many-to-one join. These dates are index-relative numbers and stay private.

death <- omop_event("death", name = "death")
hazard <- omop_recipe(events = list(lab, death), populations = list(entry), variables = list(
  next_day = omop_variable(event = lab,
    reducer = omop_reduce("first_date", window = omop_window(1, NULL))),
  death_day = omop_variable(event = death, reducer = omop_reduce("first_date"))),
  outputs = list(
    omop_output("daily", rows = "entry", format = "person_period",
      options = list(sources = list(lab), bins = list(width = 1L),
        window = omop_window(1, 7300), analyses = "count", representation = "dense")),
    omop_output("ends", rows = "entry", format = "wide"),
    omop_output("risk", rows = "entry", format = "joined",
      options = list(from = list(list(output = "daily"), list(output = "ends")),
        how = "left", cardinality = "many_to_one"))))
hazard$publish <- "risk"
book_symbols(recipe_execute(hazard, out = c(risk = "D_days"), conns = two_conns, symbol = "book_pool"))
#>     risk 
#> "D_days"

Remove days after the first repeat or death. A missing next-day value means “no subsequent lab found”, so retain observed days until another censor applies. We count an event on the death day if both dates coincide; state this tie rule.

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_days", to_next = next_day - period_start_days,
  to_death = death_day - period_start_days,
  newobj = "D_remaining", conns = two_conns, symbol = "book_pool"))
#> [1] "D_remaining"
print(ds.omop.filter("D_remaining",
  expr = omop_where((is.na(to_next) | to_next >= 0) &
  (is.na(to_death) | to_death >= 0)),
  newobj = "D_risk", conns = two_conns, symbol = "book_pool"))
#> [1] "D_risk"
print(ds.omop.mutate("D_risk", event = ifelse(hb_count > 0, 1L, 0L),
  years = period_start_days / 365.25,
  newobj = "D_hazard", conns = two_conns, symbol = "book_pool"))
#> [1] "D_hazard"
hazard_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_hazard$event", datasources = two_conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(hazard_counts))
Category Count
0 48535
1 25
NA 0

Each row is one observed day at risk. More than one lab on that day is still one outcome. Time in years is a predictor; the outcome probability remains per day. The binomial GLM models log odds with a linear time trend. A study would assess that time specification and the assumption of noninformative censoring.

The dsBase 6.3.5 local setup fits use one iteration and emit the explained glm.fit: algorithm did not converge warnings. The distributed fit then iterates; inspect its final diagnostics, which the book checks against a central fit of the public source. The warnings below are retained, not treated as evidence of success.

hazard_fit <- dsBaseClient::ds.glm("event ~ years", data = "D_hazard",
  family = "binomial", datasources = two_conns)
#> Warning: glm.fit: algorithm did not converge

hazard_table[["p-value"]] <- format.pval(hazard_table[["p-value"]], digits = 3, eps = 1e-16)
knitr::kable(hazard_table, digits = 4)
Estimate Std. Error z-value p-value

     disclosure_risk = hazard_fit$disclosure.risk, errors = hazard_fit$errorMessage)

This is a jointly estimated distributed GLM. Its risk-set likelihood has one first event at most per person; it is not a logistic model of every recurrent reading treated as an independent patient.

Exercise. Show the fitted odds ratio per additional year since entry. Does it mean a yearly probability of getting a lab?

Solution

exp(hazard_fit$coefficients["years", 1])
#> [1] 3.649034

No. It compares the odds of a repeat on the current day, conditional on having remained at risk, for a one-year difference in time since entry. It is not a causal effect or an annual risk. The event is recorded care, not disease onset.

Repeated measures and mixed models

For actual repeated-value modelling use Synthea’s BMI readings, whose within-person trajectories provide a more useful random-intercept example than hemoglobin here. A random intercept lets people have different baseline levels and accounts for correlation between their repeated readings. This is a different question from time to the first repeat lab.

bmi <- omop_event("measurement", concepts = 3038553L, value = "value_as_number",
  where = omop_where(unit_concept_id == 9531L), name = "bmi")
bmi_entry <- omop_population("bmi_entry", index = omop_index(bmi))
repeated <- omop_recipe(events = list(bmi), populations = list(bmi_entry),
  outputs = omop_output("long", rows = "bmi_entry", format = "long", sources = "bmi",
    options = list(columns_derived = c("value", "unit", "days_since_previous"))))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(repeated, out = c(long = "D_long"), conns = two_conns, symbol = "book_pool"))
#>     long 
#> "D_long"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_long", datasources = two_conns)
#> $north
#>  [1] "row_id"                      "cohort_row_id"              
#>  [3] "person_id"                   "concept_id"                 
#>  [5] "start_date"                  "end_date"                   
#>  [7] "measurement_type_concept_id" "value_as_concept_id"        
#>  [9] "meas_event_field_concept_id" "days_since_previous"        
#> [11] "value"                       "unit_concept_id"            
#> 
#> $south
#>  [1] "row_id"                      "cohort_row_id"              
#>  [3] "person_id"                   "concept_id"                 
#>  [5] "start_date"                  "end_date"                   
#>  [7] "measurement_type_concept_id" "value_as_concept_id"        
#>  [9] "meas_event_field_concept_id" "days_since_previous"        
#> [11] "value"                       "unit_concept_id"

start_date is days since first BMI under the default relative-date policy. The person key, all readings and their dates stay on the servers. Preserve actual time; coding visit numbers as equally spaced would misrepresent these records. Each person has exactly one indexed episode here, so cohort_row_id is the person-level grouping key for these models. Using this stable episode key also keeps the local teaching runs reproducible when temporary resource paths change pseudonym labels. With multiple episodes per person, use a person-level key to model their dependence instead.

print(ds.omop.mutate("D_long", years = start_date / 365.25,
  above_cutoff = ifelse(value >= 25, 1L, 0L),
  newobj = "D_repeat", conns = two_conns, symbol = "book_pool"))
#> [1] "D_repeat"
repeat_mean <- dsBaseClient::ds.mean("D_repeat$value", type = "combine", datasources = two_conns)
repeat_counts <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_repeat$above_cutoff", datasources = two_conns)
knitr::kable(book_group_comparison(repeat_counts, repeat_mean, "BMI reading", "kg/m²"))
Category Count Number Unit Mean
0 123 BMI reading kg/m² 25.76941
1 315 BMI reading kg/m² 25.76941
NA 0 BMI reading kg/m² 25.76941

This mean weights readings, not people. The cutoff is a teaching rule only: this synthetic population includes children, and an adult BMI cutoff is not an age-specific clinical classification. The continuous and binary responses answer different questions.

SLMA means study-level meta-analysis. Each server fits its own mixed model; only estimates and standard errors return for pooling. It is not a single mixed model fitted jointly to concatenated rows. Here we show fixed-effect meta-analysis columns (pooled.FE, se.FE); this assumes a common coefficient across sites. The method also returns ML/REML random-effects pooling, with little information about between-site heterogeneity from only two sites.

The installed dsBase calls lme4::nobars, which in this dependency version emits a deprecation warning about moving to reformulas. It concerns the upstream API, not the data. We retain and explain that exact warning; model convergence and singularity are checked separately rather than suppressing diagnostics.

linear_mixed <- dsBaseClient::ds.lmerSLMA("value ~ years + (1|cohort_row_id)",
  dataName = "D_repeat", datasources = two_conns)
#> Warning: the 'nobars' function has moved to the reformulas package. Please update your
#> imports, or ask an upstream package maintainer to do so.
knitr::kable(linear_mixed$SLMA.pooled.ests.matrix[, c("pooled.FE", "se.FE"), drop = FALSE])
pooled.FE se.FE
(Intercept) 23.3504584 0.9636351
years 0.1507029 0.0153574 
linear_mixed$Convergence.error.message
#> [1] "Study1: no convergence error reported" "Study2: no convergence error reported"

The time coefficient is BMI units per year under this linear trajectory model. Real growth may be nonlinear; these data do not validate a constant-slope assumption. No individual random intercepts are downloaded.

binary_mixed <- dsBaseClient::ds.glmerSLMA("above_cutoff ~ years + (1|cohort_row_id)",
  family = "binomial", dataName = "D_repeat", datasources = two_conns)
knitr::kable(binary_mixed$SLMA.pooled.ests.matrix[, c("pooled.FE", "se.FE"), drop = FALSE])
pooled.FE se.FE
(Intercept) 4.7059447 2.6100909
years 0.0093367 0.0526681 
binary_mixed$Convergence.error.message
#> [1] "Study1: no convergence error reported" "Study2: no convergence error reported"

This coefficient is on the log-odds scale for a reading above the teaching cutoff, conditional on the person’s random intercept. It is neither a BMI-unit slope nor the first-event hazard from the preceding section.

Exercise 1. Show the number of contributing sites and the binary-model time odds ratio. Is SLMA pooling equivalent to the preceding distributed GLM?

Solution 1

list(sites = binary_mixed$num.valid.studies,
     time_odds_ratio = exp(binary_mixed$SLMA.pooled.ests.matrix["years", "pooled.FE"]))
#> $sites
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $time_odds_ratio
#> [1] 1.00938

No. SLMA combines site coefficients and their uncertainty. The distributed GLM combines iteration statistics to estimate one model. Both need compatible variable meaning and disjoint populations; they solve different estimation problems.

Exercise 2. Would a singular fit be proof that a mixed model worked well?

Solution 2

No. A near-zero random-effect variance or another boundary estimate can make the random-effects structure unsupported. Inspect the site’s convergence messages, variance components, observation counts and design. Simplify or reconsider the model for a reason; do not remove warnings merely to obtain a clean table.

Recap

Choose the row meaning first. Keep actual time for irregular readings; distinguish missing values, absent events and time outside observation. Request the recipe’s shape when possible, and understand what information a reshape cannot recover. A first-event hazard needs an at-risk panel with follow-up stopped at the event. Repeated-measure models instead retain repeated readings and model their dependence. Check every site’s diagnostics and distinguish joint GLM estimation from SLMA pooling.
